claim: Keep Common Crawl's CCBot unblocked: its monthly open web snapshot feeds the training data of major AI models, so blocking it removes the store from that pipeline.
body: Many stores and bot-protection settings block crawlers broadly, and some brands deliberately block AI bots. The speaker's argument is that Common Crawl's crawler, CCBot, builds a monthly open snapshot of the web that AI labs download and filter for model training, so being crawlable by it is how a brand's facts can end up inside future models, while retrieval-time agents determine whether the brand is cited in live answers. Both need access. How to apply: check robots.txt, firewall and bot-management rules for CCBot and the main AI search and assistant agents, and allow the ones you want; make key product, comparison and policy pages fast and readable without heavy client-side rendering, since he says slow pages fare badly with AI fetchers; keep content fresh. Decide deliberately rather than by default: a brand that does not want its content used for training may still allow retrieval agents. Verify agent user agents and IP ranges against each operator's published documentation, because spoofed user agents are common. His figure that about 60 percent of searches are now agent-driven is unsourced.
conditions: Any ecommerce site using bot management, a WAF or robots.txt rules, especially those that block unknown crawlers by default.
fails_when: Brands with legal or licensing reasons to keep content out of training data; sites under scraping attack where a spoofed CCBot user agent must be verified before allowing.
numbers: Common Crawl snapshot built monthly

claim: About 5.9% of 140 million sites block GPTBot, often by accident; Cloudflare's robots.txt AI-bot setting is on by default, so check robots.txt for AI crawler disallows.
body: Ahrefs found roughly 5.9% of 140 million websites blocking OpenAI's GPTBot in robots.txt. Many did not mean to: rules are inherited from old templates, and Cloudflare has a feature that manages AI bot traffic through robots.txt which is now enabled by default, adding disallow rules without the owner editing anything. A blocked assistant crawler cannot read your pages, which caps how often you are cited or recommended, however good the content. The 30-second check: open yourdomain.com/robots.txt and look for disallow lines next to GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot and Google-Extended. Decide deliberately per bot: search and citation crawlers (OAI-SearchBot and similar) send discovery and referral traffic; training crawlers (GPTBot, Google-Extended) feed future models. Some brands allow search bots and block training bots. If you sit behind Cloudflare, review its AI crawler controls as well as the file itself. Recheck after any theme change, platform migration or CDN setting change, since these can rewrite the file.
conditions: Any store wanting assistant citations, especially sites behind Cloudflare or migrated from older templates.
fails_when: The brand has decided to block training crawlers for content-licensing or copying reasons; then block training bots specifically while leaving search and citation bots open, rather than allowing everything.
numbers: about 5.9% of 140 million sites block GPTBot

claim: AVS is off by default in Shopify Payments because fraud analysis already screens risk; turning it on can raise false declines, so review order risk reports first.
body: In Shopify Payments the fraud prevention settings are at Settings, Payments, Shopify Payments, Manage, Fraud prevention. There you can require address verification (AVS) and CVV and choose how checkout handles a billing address that does not match. Shopify's guide notes AVS is switched off by default because the built-in fraud analysis already handles high-risk transactions separately, and that enabling AVS on top of it can increase false declines of legitimate orders (for example customers whose bank holds an old address). So the order of work is: first look at the order risk reports to see how many fraudulent orders actually get through and at what risk level; then decide whether stricter AVS rules are worth losing some good customers. Handle the gap with automation instead of blanket rules: in Shopify Flow, use the order risk triggers to auto-capture low-risk orders, send internal alerts for medium risk, put high-risk orders in a manual review queue, and cancel orders matching known fraud patterns. Flow includes pre-built fraud workflow templates.
conditions: Shopify stores using Shopify Payments and its fraud analysis.

claim: Most card processors flag merchants whose chargeback rate passes 0.9%, and above 1% can stop accepting their cards; each chargeback costs about $128 in fees and internal costs.
body: Shopify's security guide gives the thresholds processors use: a chargeback rate above about 0.9% of transactions gets a store flagged, and above 1% processors can stop accepting cards altogether, which for an online store means it cannot take payment. Each chargeback costs on average $128 in third-party fees and internal handling, on top of the lost product and revenue. Card-not-present fraud usually starts with card testing, where fraudsters run small orders to check stolen numbers before larger fraud, so a sudden run of small, unusual orders is an early warning before chargebacks arrive weeks later. The worked customer example: Maine Lobster Now had fraud chargebacks at 0.25% of transactions and after moving to Shopify Payments with integrated fraud tools fell to 0.025%, a 93% reduction. How to use it: track chargeback rate weekly as a share of transactions, set an internal alert well below 0.9% (for example 0.5%), investigate card-testing patterns immediately, and when the rate rises tighten verification (3D Secure, CVV, risk-based order review) before the processor acts. Confirm the exact thresholds with your own processor, since card network programmes and processor rules differ.
conditions: Card-accepting online stores; thresholds as stated by Shopify for most processors.

claim: Shopify Payments applies 3D Secure only to higher-risk transactions; an authenticated payment shifts fraud chargeback liability to the card issuer. Only 32.4% of stores use 3DS.
body: 3D Secure adds a one-time code or biometric check at payment. Shopify Payments applies it dynamically: only higher-risk transactions see the extra step, so most legitimate customers check out without friction. When a cardholder completes 3DS, liability for a fraudulent chargeback on that transaction moves from the store to the card issuer, so Visa and Mastercard fraud disputes on authenticated payments are no longer the merchant's loss. Shopify cites that only 32.4% of store owners use 3DS at all. Alongside it, Shopify's machine-learning fraud analysis scores every order low, medium or high risk using AVS, CVV, IP address, proxy detection and unusual patterns, and eligible US stores on Shopify Payments can use Shopify Protect, which guarantees payment on protected orders and covers the chargeback and dispute fee. When choosing any other gateway, Shopify's checklist is PCI DSS certification at the processor level, tokenisation of card data and support for 3DS 2.0. For a store paying off fraud chargebacks, check whether risk-based 3DS is active before adding blanket friction such as CAPTCHAs or manual review of every order.
conditions: Stores on Shopify Payments (dynamic 3DS); liability shift applies to authenticated card transactions; Shopify Protect only for eligible US merchants.
numbers: 32.4% of store owners implement 3DS (as cited by Shopify)

claim: Stores processing under 20,000 card transactions a year are PCI Level 4 (annual self-assessment); on Shopify the merchant's job is never storing card numbers outside checkout.
body: PCI DSS has 12 core requirements and applies to every business that accepts cards, whatever its size. Most small online stores fall into Level 4, defined in the guide as fewer than 20,000 transactions a year, which requires an annual self-assessment questionnaire rather than a formal third-party audit. Shopify says self-hosted stores also face quarterly vulnerability scans and sometimes a qualified assessor, costing small businesses roughly $1,000 to $10,000 a year. On Shopify, compliance is handled at platform level, and the merchant's responsibility is not to introduce card data anywhere else: never ask customers for card details outside checkout, and never store card numbers in order notes, emails or spreadsheets. The other merchant-side duties under Shopify's shared responsibility model: two-step authentication on every admin account, not just the owner (required for Shopify Payments; passkeys supported); audit installed apps in Settings, Apps and sales channels, removing unused ones and checking each app's data permissions; prefer apps with Built for Shopify status and review scores above 3.75; and train staff on phishing, which IBM's 2025 report names as the most common breach entry point at 16%.
conditions: Shopify-hosted stores; Level 4 threshold as described in the guide (card brand rules govern the exact levels).

claim: Gate AI agents by action, not identity: let them browse freely, and apply verification only at checkout, account changes, loyalty redemption and gift-card balance checks.
body: Blanket bot blocking now costs sales: legitimate shopping agents (ChatGPT, Perplexity and in-browser agents) browse headlessly, fail honeypots and invisible CAPTCHAs, and get falsely declined, while sophisticated malicious automation mimics human behaviour well enough to pass. Akamai reported AI bots at nearly 48 percent of commerce traffic on its network as of December 2025, and vendors report most AI bot traffic passing unrestricted because sites cannot tell agents apart. The practical model is a four-step ladder tied to what the visitor is trying to do: permit low-risk actions (catalogue, search, product pages, reviews); verify when behaviour shifts (a sudden burst of add-to-carts or price page sweeps); challenge with step-up authentication or an AI-resistant challenge for risky actions (checkout, address or email change, loyalty points, gift card balance checks); prevent known-malicious patterns (card testing, credential stuffing, inventory hoarding on drops). Start by listing which agents visit which pages, write a short policy of allowed, rate-limited and blocked actions, then enforce it at the CDN or bot-management layer rather than in theme code.
conditions: Stores receiving AI agent traffic and using a CDN or bot-management product (Cloudflare, Shopify's built-in bot protection, Akamai, DataDome or similar); most urgent for brands with product drops, gift cards or loyalty balances.
fails_when: Sites under an active credential-stuffing or card-testing attack, where temporarily tightening everything is correct until the attack subsides; and very small stores whose platform gives no per-action control, where platform defaults are the practical limit.

claim: Lock down your own AI shopping assistant: no authority to override prices or policies, rate limits, and alerts for token freeloading, where bots route workloads through your endpoint.
body: A store's public AI chatbot is a new attack surface. Two patterns from the report: first, 'leaky faucet' probing, where automated agents systematically vary inputs to talk a chatbot into breaking business rules (issuing discounts, approving refunds, revealing other customers' order data); second, token freeloading, where bot networks send their own processing or model queries through a retailer's public AI endpoint, running up the retailer's model bill and degrading service for real shoppers. Prompt injection hidden in content the assistant reads (reviews, forum posts, product Q&A) can also redirect it. Controls: (1) the assistant should read policy and catalogue data but have no write authority over prices, discounts, refunds or addresses; route those to deterministic systems or a human; (2) require authentication and step-up before it touches any order or account; (3) rate-limit per session and per IP, cap response length and spend, and block off-topic requests; (4) sanitise user and third-party text before it reaches the model; (5) monitor cost per conversation and alert on spikes, which flag freeloading early.
conditions: Stores running an LLM-powered chatbot, support agent or shopping assistant on their site or in support channels.
fails_when: Stores using a hosted support bot whose vendor already enforces scoping and rate limits; controls still need checking but not building. Over-restricting can make the assistant useless, so scope by action rather than disabling it.

claim: Treat cryptographic agent identity (Web Bot Auth, Visa Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Agent Pay) as a passport, not a pass: keep monitoring and stop verified agents whose intent drifts.
body: Agent identity standards let a well-behaved agent prove who it is and whom it acts for: Web Bot Auth uses HTTP message signatures, Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol (built with Cloudflare and supported by processors and Shopify) signs the agent's identity and stated intent, Mastercard Agent Pay and Know-Your-Agent token schemes do similar for payments. Verification answers who; it does not answer what the agent is doing now. The model the report describes is passport plus immigration officer: the protocol is the passport, and edge behavioural monitoring checks origin and in-session behaviour. A verified agent arriving from a compromised server, or one that declared browsing intent and then starts scraping prices or testing card numbers, is challenged or removed. How to apply: (1) turn on your CDN's verified-bot and signed-agent recognition so known shopping agents are not falsely declined; (2) give verified agents a dedicated, rate-limited path (an agent rail) with only the permissions each action needs; (3) keep velocity and fraud rules active for them at checkout and account endpoints; (4) review agent traffic monthly as the standards are still settling.
conditions: Stores expecting agentic checkout traffic in 2026 and later; CDN or payment stack that supports signed agent recognition (Cloudflare, Akamai, Stripe, Adyen, Shopify).
fails_when: Standards and vendor support are still changing quickly, so specific protocol names may be superseded; small stores relying on platform-managed checkout cannot configure agent rails themselves and should use platform settings.

claim: A CAPTCHA alone will not stop a determined bot: human solving services have sold about 1,000 solves for $0.50, while each one costs a real shopper about 10 seconds.
body: A CAPTCHA tries to prove a human is present, but attackers rent humans. Solving services take the challenge image from the target site, have low-paid workers or lured users answer it in real time, and return the answer through an API, priced at around 50 cents per 1,000 solves in the lecture's example. Older text CAPTCHAs were also beaten by software: a 2003 paper broke two common open-source versions 92% and 33% of the time, and researchers treat even 1% as broken because attackers get several tries. Meanwhile each challenge costs a genuine visitor about 10 seconds and is hard for people with visual impairments. Invisible, score-based checks (such as reCAPTCHA's background mode) avoid the friction by building a reputation from behaviour and IP history, but they penalise privacy-focused visitors on shared or anonymising IPs. How to apply: do not put a CAPTCHA on every login or checkout; show one only as a step-up after a rate limit or risk score trips, prefer score-based checks for routine traffic, and rely on rate limits, breached-password checks and 2FA as the main controls.
conditions: Storefront login, account creation, checkout or form endpoints facing automated abuse; figures date from the lecture series (likely around 2019) and solve prices change.
fails_when: Low-value, low-volume attacks where any challenge deters the attacker; score-based checks flag legitimate shoppers on VPNs or privacy browsers and cost conversions.

claim: Set login rate limits per username and per IP at about 10x what the most extreme real user would do, because one office or carrier IP can carry 100 people.
body: Brute force (many passwords on one account), credential stuffing (username and password pairs from another site's breach) and password spraying (one weak password across many accounts) all depend on making many login attempts quickly, so capping attempts is the first defence. Count attempts both per username and per IP address: per username stops brute force on one account, per IP stops one machine trying many accounts. The risk is blocking real customers, since a corporate network or mobile carrier can put around a hundred people behind one IP. The lecturer's rule of thumb is to set the limit about an order of magnitude above the most extreme legitimate behaviour you can imagine, then raise it if you see real users blocked. When the limit trips, either delay the response or return a 'too many requests' error, and offer a human check so a real user can continue. The same limit lets you show friendlier 'no account with this email' messages without letting attackers check thousands of emails. Add breached-password checks and a second factor for unrecognised devices on top.
conditions: Self-hosted or custom storefronts and customer-account logins (for example WooCommerce or headless builds) where the merchant controls login handling; hosted platforms handle much of this themselves.
fails_when: Attacks spread across many residential IPs (low per-IP rates), so per-IP limits miss them; limits set too low lock out shared-network customers; the platform already rate-limits and a second layer just adds friction.
numbers: limit about 10x the most extreme legitimate user
about 100 users can share one corporate IP
